en.title: Comparing people
en.summary: How to compare two people, or one person with a group.

paragraphs: We often compare people when we describe them. Here is a short text about three friends.
Tom is taller than Ben, but Ben is stronger. Anna is the youngest of the three. She is also the cleverest, and she is more serious than the boys. Ben is the funniest person I know.

**1. The comparative uses -er or more, and than.** Add -er to short adjectives: taller. Use more with long adjectives: more serious. Name the second person with than. See Introduction to Grammar: Adjectives and comparison.

blocks.html:
AdjectiveComparativeExample
talltallerTom is taller than Ben.
strongstrongerBen is stronger.
seriousmore seriousAnna is more serious.

paragraphs: **2. The superlative uses the and -est or most.** Use the superlative to say that one person is first in a group: the youngest, the cleverest, the funniest. Use of or in to name the group. See Introduction to Grammar: Adjectives and comparison.

blocks.html:
AdjectiveSuperlativeExample
youngthe youngestAnna is the youngest of the three.
cleverthe cleverestShe is the cleverest.
funnythe funniestBen is the funniest.

items: Use **as... as** to say that two people are equal: **Tom is as tall as Ben.**
Adjectives ending in a consonant and y change y to i: **funny**, **funnier**, **the funniest**.
In everyday English, people say **taller than me**, not taller than I.

paragraphs: In English-speaking cultures, comparisons between people are usually made in a friendly way, and a gentle joke is common between friends.
